question: Where does a gesture's time actually go once the evidence preamble is carried?
howThisWasFound: The plan was a persistent dispatch channel. Before building it, the Runtime's
own per-gesture cost was measured with the device answered by a zero-cost fake.
It came back at p50 245ms / p95 392ms - nearly the whole 400ms interaction
budget, before any device work at all. So the transport was not the bottleneck
and the channel would have optimised the smaller half.
rootCause: A session-scoped capability is one record, as intended - but its `consumptions`
array grows by one entry per gesture, and the whole store document is encoded
and rewritten atomically on each consume and again on each outcome.
So the cost of taking one use grew with how many uses that capability had
already taken: quadratic over a session, in the exact place the session scope

storeCostPerUse.note: one consume + one recordOutcome, measured directly against the store

before.finding: past roughly use 400 a single authorization exceeds the whole 400ms gesture budget on its own

runtimePerGesture.note: engine submit + run, device answered by a zero-cost fake

after.residualSlope: 96->118ms over 200 gestures, from checkpoint amortisation over a growing document; bounded, not quadratic

design: The document is a checkpoint; each use is appended to a durable ledger and
fsynced. Load = checkpoint + replay of the events appended since. The document
is written out whole every 128 events, which is what bounds replay.
The parsed document is cached in memory and reused only while both files are
byte-for-byte the ones it was built from, so another writer's change is never
safetyProperties: A final line without its newline is a torn append: the use never became durable,
so the tail is dropped rather than half-read into an authorization.
A reservation appearing twice in replay fails closed as storeCorrupted rather
than spending the use twice - the window a crash between a checkpoint and its
Replayed state is validated as a whole, exactly as a checkpoint is, so a
tampered receipt digest in the ledger fails closed the same way it did in the
Full durability is preserved: every receipt is still kept, per the maintainer's
earlier ruling. Only where it is written changed.

provenInTests.testTakingAUseDoesNotRewriteTheWholeStor: twenty uses leave the document byte-identical
provenInTests.testAReopenedStoreSeesEveryAppendedUse: a fresh store on the same directory sees exactly what the writer saw
provenInTests.testATornFinalAppendIsDiscardedNotGuesse: a half-written final line does not become a use
provenInTests.testAReplayedReservationFailsClosed: a duplicated consume event is refused, not double-spent
provenInTests.testTheLedgerIsBoundedByPeriodicCheckpoi: past the threshold the ledger resets and no use is lost
provenInTests.testAnotherWritersUseIsNeverServedFromMe: a warm cache never hides another writer's use
provenInTests.negativeControl: with appends forced back to whole-document rewrites, 5 assertions across 3 of these fail

portedFixtures: Two existing tests recreated durability windows by hand-editing the document.
The window now lives in the ledger, so they were ported to it - which models the
real crash (an append that never landed) more directly than editing a document.

reading: p50 now sits just inside the gate; p95 does not.
The persistent dispatch channel measures 66ms on the uinput leg (242 -> 177ms)
and is what turns 'just inside' into comfortable. It is the next step, and it
is now worth its hazards - which it was not while the Runtime spent 245ms.
